title: The fourth fleet's captain underlines his own log
summary: Off the north-west cape the watch of the fourth fleet's own hull reports a thing longer than her own keel moving beneath a clear sea; the captain sets down what his watch told him, underlines the line twice, and writes beneath it that he has called it a whale.

title: Anna nic Phàil cuts a page of figures from her own draft
summary: Writing her motion at her own table through the early months of the year, Anna nic Phàil cuts a whole page of named costs, granaries and flooded pit-heads and the stone at Cathair mhòr, judging that a council grows deaf to a column of figures faster than to almost anything else brought before it.

title: The master of the Treasury asks a figure of the motion
summary: Uisdean Dubh, master of the Treasury, asks Anna nic Phàil's motion for amends whether its sum has been costed against the year's roll; she answers that the reckoning is the room's own trade, and asks only that the principle be granted.

title: The motion held over, morning after morning
summary: For eight sittings running the council's clerk carries the motion for amends forward on the day's business-paper under the same two words, held over, without any member speaking against it or any vote being called.

title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is asked whether the sum is too great
summary: Caught at the chamber door, Somhairle mac Lachlainn tells Anna nic Phàil that he has read many rolls of the dead and never once been asked whether the towns that raised them could bear the cost, and does not know why a roll of the dead should be easier to pay for than a roll of the living.

title: The motion stood over without a sitting called
summary: On the eighth day the motion for amends is absent from the business-paper; a clerk tells Anna nic Phàil it was stood over to the autumn sitting the evening before, in a short session she was not told was sitting, by members' vote without her among them.

title: Anna counts the councillors who looked away
summary: Going back over the eight sittings, Anna nic Phàil can find no single vote that killed the motion, only the faces of the twelve, one who promised a vote and never called it, one who spoke of hard times, six who said nothing to her at all, and Somhairle who gave her an answer and moved no more than the rest to call it to a vote.

title: Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale she means to lay the chair down
summary: In the delegates' room over the net-lofts at Caol mhòr, Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale plainly that she means to lay down the Moot's chair that year, and that she judges him, of every delegate she has sat among, the fittest to take it up.

title: Martha Greaves's last sitting
summary: Martha Greaves reads out the year's register and the ordinary business of the day, a roof at the school, the price of wool, a mill's complaint of the coal-line's freight, lays the chair down, and the Moot chooses Peter Hale by acclamation without a show of hands.

title: Martha Greaves goes home to Doire ghlas
summary: Martha Greaves rides home to Doire ghlas on the ordinary carrier's cart with no more baggage than she came to the mill with as a young woman, not yet certain what a woman who was the Moot's own voice for seventeen years is to do with her mornings now.

title: The fifth regiment raises stone barracks at Seann Warr
summary: The fifth regiment, quartered under canvas and borrowed roofs since the war's first summer, raises a barracks of dressed stone on ground the town of Seann Warr gives freely, judging a regiment likely to stay worth more to its trade settled than tented.

title: The Seann Spioradan house of Inis uaine prays for the eighth regiment
summary: The eighth regiment's watch on the eastern dubhan tanks is made lasting with officers' houses in the town rather than borrowed sheds, and the Seann Spioradan house of Inis uaine, never before asked to name a company of soldiers, adds it to its Sunday round.

title: The fourth regiment marches home to Caol bheag
summary: The fourth regiment leaves the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr, its colours cased at last for the journey home to Caol bheag, four years after it was first quartered there over the Moot's own protest.

title: The magistrate's house is given to the maor
summary: The Moot asks that the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr be given to the town it stands in; the council grants the house within the season, but to the maor who governs the town in the kingdom's name, not to the town itself.

title: Officers' houses at Inis uaine
summary: By council order the eighth regiment's officers at Inis uaine are given houses in the town in place of quarters borrowed year by year from the tank-yard's sheds.

title: The quarrymen of Seann Warr
summary: The quarrymen of Seann Warr cut the stone for the fifth regiment's barracks through the summer from the same face that gave the harbour wall, and are paid by the Treasury at a rate the town's masons call fair.

title: Cnoc bhàn's harbour opened again
summary: The Tuathaich of Cnoc bhàn open their harbour again to boats they do not know, the raiders who took the salt-boats having been brought into Seann Skell.

title: The springs of Muileann ruadh in a wet summer
summary: The hot springs below Muileann ruadh run so full in the wet summer that the bath-house's lower room floods, and the custodians carry the sick up to the long room.
